Title: Francis Watson
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
**Francis Watson** (born 1956) is an English New Testament scholar, Professor in the Department of Theology and Religion at Durham University, and a critic of the New Perspective on Paul known for arguing that theological concerns belong inside, not outside, biblical scholarship.12

## Life and Ministry
Watson earned an MA and a DPhil from Oxford, completing his doctorate in 1984.1 He began his academic career at King’s College London before his appointment in 1999 to the Kirby Laing Chair of New Testament Exegesis at the University of Aberdeen. In 2007 he moved to Durham University, where he holds his current professorship in the Department of Theology and Religion.1

## Theological Contribution
Watson’s early monograph, _Paul, Judaism, and the Gentiles: A Sociological Approach_ (1986), read Paul’s letters through the social dynamics of the early Christian communities that produced them. He revised and expanded this work as _Paul, Judaism, and the Gentiles: Beyond the New Perspective_ (2007), a title announcing his break from a position he had once shared.2 Aaron Thomas O’Kelley’s 2010 dissertation on the New Perspective on Paul describes Watson, “although formerly identified with the new perspective,” as someone who “now seeks to move beyond it,” and quotes a 2001 essay in which Watson laid out the New Perspective’s characteristic three-step argument before rejecting it: readers first notice Paul contrasting the gospel’s grace with a Jewish or Jewish-Christian law-keeping, then are told this cannot really be an antithesis between divine and human agency because “Sanders has taught us that Judaism was and is a religion of grace,” and are therefore pushed to read Paul’s “faith” and “works” language as a claim about who belongs to the people of God rather than about how a person is saved.2 In _Paul and the Hermeneutics of Faith_ (2004), Watson argued that Leviticus 18:5, which Paul quotes in Galatians 3:12, states the law’s own “entire rationale” in a single sentence, and that the assumption that “life” there presupposes sinless, perfect obedience is, in his view, “irrelevant to Paul’s argument” and even “contradicts Leviticus itself.” Jason DeRouchie’s 2020 _Themelios_ article and Micah John McCormick’s 2010 dissertation both take up and dispute this specific reading of Leviticus 18:5.34

## Theological Contribution
Watson has also written extensively on biblical theology’s own theological method, in _Text, Church, and World: Biblical Interpretation in Theological Perspective_ (1994) and _Text and Truth: Redefining Biblical Theology_ (1997). Michael Kruger’s _The Question of Canon_ (2013) reports that “Francis Watson has pressed the case that, ‘Theological concerns should have an acknowledged place within the field of biblical scholarship,’” in the course of arguing that the canon itself is inescapably a theological, not merely historical, question.5 Kruger elsewhere credits Watson with tracing the modern scholarly suspicion of early Christian writing, over against oral proclamation, to the existentialism of Friedrich Schleiermacher and Rudolf Bultmann. Watson, as Kruger presents him, calls this suspicion a “neo-Marcionite rejection of Judaism,” since it identifies the written text with “Jewishness, the letter that kills,” and treats the recovery of an unwritten, immediate gospel as a purification of Christianity from its Jewish, textual roots.6 Andreas Köstenberger’s survey of the discipline reports a taxonomy of biblical theology, proposed by Edward Klink and Darian Lockett, that runs from “more theological” to “more historical” and names Watson as the sole representative of its most theological type, “Biblical Theology as Theological Construction,” alongside James Barr, D. A. Carson, N. T. Wright, and Brevard Childs as the representatives of the other four.7 Watson continued this project into Gospel studies in later monographs, including _Gospel Writing: A Canonical Perspective_ (2013) and _What Is a Gospel?_ (2022).

## Historical Significance
Watson retitled his own 1986 monograph _Beyond the New Perspective_ in 2007, announcing a break from a position he once held. O’Kelley treats Watson’s own account, that the New Perspective’s Pauline grace/law antitheses are really claims about Jew-Gentile ecclesiology rather than about divine and human agency, as independent confirmation, from a scholar who once held the position himself, that the movement rests on an assumption from Sanders it has never actually argued for.2 Kruger draws on Watson’s case that theological concerns belong within biblical scholarship, alongside similar arguments from Iain Provan, Floyd Filson, and Kevin Vanhoozer, in arguing that the canon is inescapably a theological question and not only a historical one.5

**Francis Watson** (born 1956) is an English theologian and New Testament scholar. He commenced his career at [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_London "King's College London") before being appointed to the Kirby Laing Chair of New Testament Exegesis at the University of Aberdeen in 1999. In 2007 he took up his current position as Professor in the Department of Theology and Religion at the Durham University.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-1)
Watson is well known as a critic of the so-called New Perspective on Paul (NPP). His criticisms of the NPP are all the more significant as he received a positive endorsement of James D. G. Dunn (a NPP proponent) for his doctoral study. After the latter endorsement, Watson explored in particular the social-scientific work of Klaus Berger which contributed to Watson changing his mind dramatically about some results of his unpublished thesis. The result was _Paul, Judaism, and the Gentiles: A Sociological Approach_, which chronicles Watson's change of mind.
Watson is also a major figure in the study of the Gospels.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-2) Watson's 2013 volume, _Gospel Writing. A Canonical Approach_, is his most voluminous study to date. Extensive critical review articles include those by Markus Bockmuehl and Richard Bauckham._[citation needed_] Watson has published _What is a Gospel?_, a sequel to the 2013 book. It emphasizes the continuity between the canonical and noncanonical Gospels as one long tradition of writing, though he finds a break between the narrative Gospels and what the Apostle Paul meant when he used the term _Gospel_. Watson has contested the existence of the hypothetical Gospel Q, instead arguing for the Farrer Hypothesis where Luke used Matthew.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-3)

Ted Dorman suggests that for Watson, "hermeneutical sovereignty resides not in the text but in the subject matter to which it points" – namely, Jesus Christ.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-4)
Watson is the editor of _New Testament Studies_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-5)
Watson's work has been endorsed by Dale Allison, Simon Gathercole, and Lewis Ayres.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-Eerdmans-6) Tucker Ferda has described _What is a Gospel_ as a "brilliant and provocative". He appreciates the main argument that the Gospels should be studied the same regardless of canonicity, though he questions whether Watson's model can fully account for the identification of the four canonical Gospels as scripture by later Christians and the claim that Paul's Gospel is distinct from other usages.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Watson_(theologian)#cite_note-7)

The **Slavery Abolition Act 1833**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-st-1) (3 & 4 Will. 4. c. 73) was an act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom which abolished slavery in the British Empire by way of compensated emancipation. The act was legislated by WhigPrime MinisterCharles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey's reforming administration, and it was enacted by ordering the British government to purchase the freedom of all slaves in the British Empire, and by outlawing the further practice of slavery in the British Empire. The act explicitly delineated 19 separate pots of compensation covering the Caribbean, South Africa, and Mauritius. Although Britain, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand were technically included, these had relatively few slaves at this time for other reasons. India was excluded. Around 800,000 freed slaves were attested in the claims process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-3)

While the 1833 Act was a landmark, it did not end slavery throughout the entire British sphere of influence. The act explicitly excluded territories like British India, where slavery was addressed separately by the Indian Slavery Act, 1843. In regions colonised later, such as Nigeria, the abolition of pre-existing local systems of slavery was a gradual process that extended into the early 20th century. Furthermore, in British protectorates, which retained their own local laws, the institution persisted for much longer. For example, slavery in Bahrain was not legally abolished until 1937.
[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument") in Newcastle upon Tyne, in remembrance of Prime Minister Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, abolisher of slavery in the British Empire

Slavery had been judged to be without legal basis in England in 1772. In May of that year, Lord Mansfield's judgment in the _Somerset_ case emancipated a slave who had been brought to England from Boston in the Province of Massachusetts Bay, and thus helped launch the movement to abolish slavery throughout the British Empire.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-5) The case ruled that slavery had no legal status in England as it had no common law or statutory law basis, and as such someone could not legally be a slave in England.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-6) However, many campaigners, including Granville Sharp, took the view that the _ratio decidendi_ of the _Somerset_ case meant that slavery was unsupported by law within England and that no ownership could be exercised on slaves entering English or Scottish soil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-8)Ignatius Sancho, who in 1774 became the second recorded black person to vote in a British general election — the first being John London — wrote a letter in 1778 that opens in praise of Britain for its "freedom, and for the many blessings I enjoy in it", before criticising the actions towards his black brethren in parts of the Empire such as the West Indies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-10)

By 1783, an anti-slavery movement to abolish the slave trade throughout the Empire had begun among the British public,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-cooley-11) with the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade being established in 1787.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-12) The Wedgwood anti-slavery medallion by Josiah Wedgwood was, according to the BBC, "the most famous image of a black person in all of 18th-century art".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-13) Fellow abolitionist Thomas Clarkson wrote: "Of the ladies several wore them in bracelets, and others had them fitted up in an ornamental manner as pins for their hair. At length, the taste for wearing them became general; and thus fashion, which usually confines itself to worthless things, was seen for once in the honourable office of promoting the cause of justice, humanity and freedom."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-14)

Spurred by an incident involving Chloe Cooley, a slave woman brought to Canada by an American loyalist, the Lieutenant-Governor of Upper Canada, John Graves Simcoe, tabled the Act Against Slavery in 1793. Passed by the local Legislative Assembly, it was the first legislation to outlaw the slave trade in a part of the British Empire.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-cooley-11) By the late 18th century, Britain was simultaneously the largest slave trader and centre of the largest abolitionist movement.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-15)William Wilberforce had written in his diary in 1787 that his great purpose in life was to suppress the slave trade before waging a 20-year fight on the industry.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-16)

# Exploring Caribbean history | "The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings | Facebook
"The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings. It also confirmed the sovereignty of King-in-Parliament over all people residing in British dominions and resolved a long-standing dispute over whether enslaved people were private property or royal subjects entitled to legal safeguards. This debate first emerged in the late eighteenth century but acquired additional urgency following the 1807 abolition of the slave trade, when attempts to mitigate slavery through the enactment of ameliorative statutes and procedural reforms encouraged enslaved people to petition magistrates for redress in cases of abuse. Slaves vigorously defended their newly granted rights to bodily protection, sustenance, and family preservation through the instigation of legal complaints against overseers, managers, and slave owners. By the 1820s, enslaved litigants across Britain’s empire were publicly and collectively petitioning colonial magistrates to intercede on their behalf. The judicialization of quotidian battles over the terms of enslavement refashioned colonial social relations, affirmed enslaved people’s status as British subjects, and generated volumes of case files that circulated back to the metropole, where the Colonial Office cited them in critical assessments of slave law and where abolitionists used them to press for immediate emancipation. Enslaved people’s legal activism was operationally antislavery; it eroded the power of colonial enslavers and prodded Parliament to pass the 1833 Abolition Act."

# Exploring Caribbean history | "The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings | Facebook
"The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings. It also confirmed the sovereignty of King-in-Parliament over all people residing in British dominions and resolved a long-standing dispute over whether enslaved people were private property or royal subjects entitled to legal safeguards. This debate first emerged in the late eighteenth century but acquired additional urgency following the 1807 abolition of the slave trade, when attempts to mitigate slavery through the enactment of ameliorative statutes and procedural reforms encouraged enslaved people to petition magistrates for redress in cases of abuse. Slaves vigorously defended their newly granted rights to bodily protection, sustenance, and family preservation through the instigation of legal complaints against overseers, managers, and slave owners. By the 1820s, enslaved litigants across Britain’s empire were publicly and collectively petitioning colonial magistrates to intercede on their behalf. The judicialization of quotidian battles over the terms of enslavement refashioned colonial social relations, affirmed enslaved people’s status as British subjects, and generated volumes of case files that circulated back to the metropole, where the Colonial Office cited them in critical assessments of slave law and where abolitionists used them to press for immediate emancipation. Enslaved people’s legal activism was operationally antislavery; it eroded the power of colonial enslavers and prodded Parliament to pass the 1833 Abolition Act."

The **Slavery Abolition Act 1833**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-st-1) (3 & 4 Will. 4. c. 73) was an act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom which abolished slavery in the British Empire by way of compensated emancipation. The act was legislated by WhigPrime MinisterCharles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey's reforming administration, and it was enacted by ordering the British government to purchase the freedom of all slaves in the British Empire, and by outlawing the further practice of slavery in the British Empire. The act explicitly delineated 19 separate pots of compensation covering the Caribbean, South Africa, and Mauritius. Although Britain, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand were technically included, these had relatively few slaves at this time for other reasons. India was excluded. Around 800,000 freed slaves were attested in the claims process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-3)
texts.1:
While the 1833 Act was a landmark, it did not end slavery throughout the entire British sphere of influence. The act explicitly excluded territories like British India, where slavery was addressed separately by the Indian Slavery Act, 1843. In regions colonised later, such as Nigeria, the abolition of pre-existing local systems of slavery was a gradual process that extended into the early 20th century. Furthermore, in British protectorates, which retained their own local laws, the institution persisted for much longer. For example, slavery in Bahrain was not legally abolished until 1937.
[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument") in Newcastle upon Tyne, in remembrance of Prime Minister Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, abolisher of slavery in the British Empire
texts.2: Slavery had been judged to be without legal basis in England in 1772. # Exploring Caribbean history | "The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings | Facebook
"The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act provided for the gradual emancipation of eight hundred thousand human beings. It also confirmed the sovereignty of King-in-Parliament over all people residing in British dominions and resolved a long-standing dispute over whether enslaved people were private property or royal subjects entitled to legal safeguards. This debate first emerged in the late eighteenth century but acquired additional urgency following the 1807 abolition of the slave trade, when attempts to mitigate slavery through the enactment of ameliorative statutes and procedural reforms encouraged enslaved people to petition magistrates for redress in cases of abuse. Slaves vigorously defended their newly granted rights to bodily protection, sustenance, and family preservation through the instigation of legal complaints against overseers, managers, and slave owners. By the 1820s, enslaved litigants across Britain’s empire were publicly and collectively petitioning colonial magistrates to intercede on their behalf. The judicialization of quotidian battles over the terms of enslavement refashioned colonial social relations, affirmed enslaved people’s status as British subjects, and generated volumes of case files that circulated back to the metropole, where the Colonial Office cited them in critical assessments of slave law and where abolitionists used them to press for immediate emancipation. Enslaved people’s legal activism was operationally antislavery; it eroded the power of colonial enslavers and prodded Parliament to pass the 1833 Abolition Act."

The **Slavery Abolition Act 1833**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-st-1) (3 & 4 Will. 4. c. 73) was an act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom which abolished slavery in the British Empire by way of compensated emancipation. The act was legislated by WhigPrime MinisterCharles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey's reforming administration, and it was enacted by ordering the British government to purchase the freedom of all slaves in the British Empire, and by outlawing the further practice of slavery in the British Empire. The act explicitly delineated 19 separate pots of compensation covering the Caribbean, South Africa, and Mauritius. Although Britain, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand were technically included, these had relatively few slaves at this time for other reasons. India was excluded. Around 800,000 freed slaves were attested in the claims process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-3)

While the 1833 Act was a landmark, it did not end slavery throughout the entire British sphere of influence. The act explicitly excluded territories like British India, where slavery was addressed separately by the Indian Slavery Act, 1843. In regions colonised later, such as Nigeria, the abolition of pre-existing local systems of slavery was a gradual process that extended into the early 20th century. Furthermore, in British protectorates, which retained their own local laws, the institution persisted for much longer. For example, slavery in Bahrain was not legally abolished until 1937.
[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument") in Newcastle upon Tyne, in remembrance of Prime Minister Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, abolisher of slavery in the British Empire

Slavery had been judged to be without legal basis in England in 1772. In May of that year, Lord Mansfield's judgment in the _Somerset_ case emancipated a slave who had been brought to England from Boston in the Province of Massachusetts Bay, and thus helped launch the movement to abolish slavery throughout the British Empire.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-5) The case ruled that slavery had no legal status in England as it had no common law or statutory law basis, and as such someone could not legally be a slave in England.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-6) However, many campaigners, including Granville Sharp, took the view that the _ratio decidendi_ of the _Somerset_ case meant that slavery was unsupported by law within England and that no ownership could be exercised on slaves entering English or Scottish soil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-8)Ignatius Sancho, who in 1774 became the second recorded black person to vote in a British general election — the first being John London — wrote a letter in 1778 that opens in praise of Britain for its "freedom, and for the many blessings I enjoy in it", before criticising the actions towards his black brethren in parts of the Empire such as the West Indies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-10)

At length, the taste for wearing them became general; and thus fashion, which usually confines itself to worthless things, was seen for once in the honourable office of promoting the cause of justice, humanity and freedom."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833#cite_note-14)

Spurred by an incident involving Chloe Cooley, a slave woman brought to Canada by an American loyalist, the Lieutenant-Governor of Upper Canada, John Graves Simcoe, tabled the Act Against Slavery in 1793.
